paragraphs.heading: Power from the tides
paragraphs.text: Tidal power takes the energy in the ocean's tides and turns it into something people can use, mostly electricity. There are several ways of doing this. It is not yet in wide use, but it could become a source of electricity in the future.

paragraphs.heading: Where the energy comes from
paragraphs.text: Tides come from tidal forces, which arise because the gravitational pull of bodies in space changes in a regular cycle. These forces set the oceans moving, so sea level rises and falls as the Earth turns. How big the swings are depends on where the Moon and Sun sit relative to Earth, on Earth's spin, and on the shape of the local seafloor and coast. Because the pattern follows Earth's rotation and the Moon's orbit, tides are more predictable than wind or sunshine.

paragraphs.heading: A different kind of energy
paragraphs.text: Tidal power is the only technology that taps energy stored in the orbits of the Earth–Moon system, and to a smaller degree the Earth–Sun system. Many other natural energies people use, such as fossil fuels, wind, waves, ordinary hydroelectric dams and solar energy, trace back to the Sun, directly or indirectly. Since the tides come from the gravity of the Moon and Sun together with Earth's rotation, the supply is practically endless. That is why tidal power is counted as renewable.

paragraphs.heading: Turbines in moving water
paragraphs.text: A tidal stream generator uses the motion of flowing water to spin turbines, much as a wind turbine uses moving air. Narrow places such as straits and inlets squeeze the water into fast currents at particular spots, and turbines placed there can catch that flow. Some generators can be fitted into existing bridges or sit fully underwater, which avoids worries about how they look.

paragraphs.heading: Dams and lagoons
paragraphs.text: A tidal barrage is a dam built right across a tidal estuary. It uses potential energy, the energy stored in the height difference between high and low tide. The rising tide fills a large basin behind the dam, and as the tide falls the water is let out through turbines that drive generators. A newer idea is a lagoon: a ring of walls with turbines built in, placed where no ecosystem existed before. Lagoons can use pumps to even out their output, and those pumps could run on surplus wind or solar power, storing energy that would otherwise be wasted.

paragraphs.heading: From mills to power stations
paragraphs.text: Tide mills were used in Europe and on North America's Atlantic coast. Water from the incoming tide was held in big ponds, and as the tide went out it turned waterwheels that ground grain. The oldest examples go back to the Middle Ages, or perhaps to Roman times. The first large-scale tidal power plant was the Rance station in France, running from 1966. It stayed the biggest by output until South Korea's Sihwa Lake station opened in August 2011, with 10 turbines producing 254 MW.

paragraphs.heading: Costs and a slowing Earth
paragraphs.text: Tidal energy has long been held back by high costs and by a shortage of sites with large enough tides or fast enough currents. Newer designs and turbines suggest much more may be available than once assumed, at costs that may become competitive. The tides themselves already drain energy from the Earth–Moon system, as water is forced through narrow coastal passages and loses energy to friction at the seabed and to turbulence, and this has slowed Earth's spin. Over the last 620 million years the day has lengthened from 21.9 to 24 hours. The extra energy taken by tidal power stations is negligible by comparison.
